{"representations":[{"case_ref":"sample_3159a77476d400f2","text":"Your main change during March 30–April 12 was a sustained drop in movement: steps averaged 2,321 versus 7,998 in your preceding 28 days (71% lower), and active time fell from 55.2 to 4.9 minutes/day (91%). Every day, including weekends, stayed below baseline, with no return by the end. Your usual 21:00 activity periods shortened from 50–60 to 0–10 minutes; intensity is unknown.

Other measurements stayed close to baseline: low movement averaged 447.5 versus 450.5 minutes, with similar daytime intervals; sleep averaged 469 versus 471 minutes, starting around 22:51 and ending at 07:00. Resting heart rate averaged 56.3 versus 56.1 bpm; RMSSD averaged 44.8 versus 45.3 ms and edged upward through the window. Higher heart-rate estimates tended to accompany lower RMSSD within this window, without establishing a cause. Activity and sleep ending the following day had only a weak association (r=0.32).

All measurements were present with qualifying coverage. Continued recording can show whether the movement reduction persists while these other measures remain stable."},{"case_ref":"sample_7de66e1de896dc00","text":"Your sleep and step counts shifted sharply and stayed lower throughout March 30–April 12, across weekdays and weekends. Recorded sleep averaged 5 hours 31 minutes versus 7 hours 49 minutes in your preceding 28 days—a reduction of 138 minutes (29%). Sleep began at 01:02–01:18 rather than 22:43–22:58, while waking remained at 07:00. Neither sleep nor steps returned toward baseline by the end.

Steps averaged 2,643 versus 7,985 (67% lower), but active time remained essentially unchanged at 55.4 versus 54.4 minutes/day, still recorded around 21:00–22:00. These movement measures therefore did not decline together; active-minute intensity is unknown. Low movement also remained similar, averaging 451 versus 449 minutes/day.

RMSSD was unchanged at 44.9 ms. Resting heart rate rose from 55 early in the window to mostly 56–57 bpm later, but its overall mean changed only from 55.9 to 56.3. Activity had little association with sleep ending the next day (r=-0.15), so these records do not explain the sleep change. All measurements had qualifying coverage and none were missing. Tracking sleep timing and steps separately would help establish whether both shifts continue."},{"case_ref":"sample_ac1d07ee01bc3c76","text":"Your sleep developed a pronounced weekday/weekend split during March 30–April 12. Your preceding 28 days averaged about 7 hours 49 minutes in both groups, with sleep beginning near 22:51 and ending at 07:00. Now, all ten weekdays recorded 6 hours 26–33 minutes, averaging 79 minutes less than baseline, with sleep starting around 00:10 and waking still at 07:00.

Both weekends instead recorded 9 hours 25–35 minutes, averaging 101 minutes more than baseline, with sleep around 01:10–11:00. The shorter weekday pattern returned on April 6 after the first longer weekend. Your overall average of 7 hours 21 minutes obscures this repeated split; the upward aggregate trend does not represent steady lengthening within weekdays.

Movement stayed close to baseline: 7,939 versus 8,019 steps and 54.7 versus 55.4 active minutes/day, with activity still around 21:00. Low movement remained near 451 minutes, although weekend intervals began at 11:30 instead of 10:00. Resting heart rate and RMSSD were also similar at 56.1 bpm and 45.4 ms. Activity showed little association with sleep ending the next day (r=-0.15). Coverage qualified throughout, with no missing measurements."},{"case_ref":"sample_0ce72b16d8a094a5","text":"Your March 30–April 12 records show a stable pattern relative to your preceding 28 days. Sleep timing remained exactly 01:00–09:00 every day, including weekends, and recorded sleep averaged 7 hours 55 minutes in both periods. Daily duration stayed within 472–479 minutes, with no sustained shortening.

Steps averaged 7,935 versus 7,963, while active time averaged 54.4 versus 53.9 minutes/day. Steps and active time showed modest upward trends within the window, although their overall levels remained near baseline. Weekends continued to have slightly more steps than weekdays (8,065 versus 7,883). Activity remained around 21:00, lasting 50–58 minutes; intensity is unknown. Low movement stayed similar at 449 versus 450 minutes/day, in repeated daytime intervals.

Your same-device resting heart-rate estimate averaged slightly lower, 55.9 versus 56.2 bpm, and RMSSD slightly higher, 45.8 versus 45.0 ms; both stayed within their baseline ranges. These small changes do not establish a broader health improvement. Activity and sleep ending the following day had only a weak inverse association (r=-0.32), and steps did not closely track active minutes. All measurements were present with qualifying coverage. Continued recording can confirm whether this consistency holds."}]}
